title: OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns
content: Eight states filed lawsuits against OpenAI on Wednesday alleging that the artificial intelligence company's ChatGPT chatbot is an unsafe product that's harmed children and deceived parents. Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana have individually sued OpenAI in their own state courts, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a release . She said Iowa's lawsuit aims to "vindicate the rights of Iowans affected by OpenAI's willful, dangerous, reckless, and unlawful conduct." "OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans," Bird said in a statement. "OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it's giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend. My lawsuit is about protecting our kids and holding OpenAI accountable under our state law." OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has built age-specific protections into its product that "many other AI products lack." He added that OpenAI is working with states to advance policies that will apply to the entire industry. "While no system can be perfect, we'll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today," Pusateri said. OpenAI is facing mounting scrutiny over its safety and security practices, including around how the company is working to protect children. In a number of wrongful death lawsuits , ChatGPT is blamed for driving users to experience harmful delusions and, in some cases, to commit suicide. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also sued OpenAI in June, alleging the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users. OpenAI has taken steps to enhance safety features for parents and children over the last year, and in August it launched a dedicated experience for minors called ChatGPT for Teens . That product includes a range of educational features and age-appropriate safeguards that are intended to reduce exposure to developmentally inappropriate or harmful content. "Teens should be able to use AI to learn, create, and explore," OpenAI said in a release at the time. "But that access should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time." If you are having suicidal thoughts or are in distress, contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 for support and assistance from a trained counselor. title: Anduril employee tender offer would value the defense tech startup at $90 billion
content: Defense tech startup Anduril will give employees a chance to sell stock through a tender offer that would value the company at roughly $90 billion, CNBC has confirmed. Bloomberg was the first to report the news, citing sources familiar with the matter. Anduril confirmed the report to CNBC. Employees participating in the offering can sell shares at $94.80 apiece. The offer, which opened on Oct. 13 and closes Nov. 9, is capped at $1.3 billion, according to the report. Bloomberg reported that employees in 16 countries are eligible to participate. Anduril has been a major winner of the growing U.S. defense tech boom and President Donald Trump 's plans to reindustrialize the U.S. military. In May, the company closed a $5 billion funding round that doubled its valuation to $61 billion. Co-founder and Oculus headset creator Palmer Luckey is among a growing group of defense tech leaders taking on advisory roles in Washington as they compete for key Department of Defense contracts. This month, the company inked a U.S. Navy shipyard contract worth up to $2.9 billion, shortly after Luckey was named a co-director of Project Meridian, which aims to develop and scale military capabilities. SpaceX rocket maker CEO Elon Musk also joined the initiative. Founded in 2017, Anduril has gained prominence for its drones, augmented reality headsets and AI software it's developing for the U.S. government and allied governments. Last month, the company made headlines after Iran said it had captured one of its underwater vehicles.

title: OpenAI’s Sachin Katti to leave infrastructure role, stay on as advisor
content: OpenAI's infrastructure lead, Sachin Katti, announced on Wednesday that he is departing his role after roughly a year at the artificial intelligence company. Katti said in a post on LinkedIn that he "decided to move on to build something new," and he'll continue to support OpenAI as an advisor after his last day on Nov. 15. Uday Ruddarraju, who has been serving as OpenAI's CTO of compute, will replace Katti and lead the company's overall compute organization, according to a spokesperson. "Building AI infrastructure at this scale has given me an incredible view into every dimension of the compute world, from silicon and systems to datacenters, energy, supply chains, financing, and the economics of AI," Katti wrote. "I'm enormously proud of what our teams accomplished together and grateful to the partners who helped make it possible." OpenAI's compute organization is crucial to its overall strategy; it's tasked with developing the company's infrastructure roadmap and ensuring that it can train and serve its models. OpenAI is targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and it's involved with massive, multi-billion-dollar data center projects in states like Ohio , Texas and Georgia . The latest leadership shakeup lands during a tense moment for AI infrastructure in the U.S., where backlash against data centers has mounted over concerns about noise, electricity rates and water consumption. The issue has become a flashpoint in the upcoming midterm elections, where both Republican and Democratic candidates have campaigned against the facilities. "I'm proud of what we've built and have total confidence in Uday and the team to carry it forward," Katti said in a statement. "I'm a builder at heart, and I'm looking forward to building something new." Ruddarraju joined OpenAI in July of last year, according to his LinkedIn. He previously served as the head of infrastructure engineering at Elon Musk's xAI, which was acquired by SpaceX earlier this year. Katti's exit is the latest in a string of executive departures at OpenAI this year. In July, Fidji Simo , OpenAI's product and business chief, said she would move into an advisory role to focus on recovery after a "severe exacerbation of a chronic illness." The following month, Brad Lightcap , a longtime OpenAI executive, and Denise Dresser , who served as revenue chief, also left the company. OpenAI President Greg Brockman told CNBC at the time that he doesn't believe the wave of departures is atypical for a young company. He said since OpenAI is in the spotlight, "every departure gets scrutinized in a way that it doesn't otherwise." "There have been different eras where we have different sets of, of leaders in place," Brockman said. "I'm a constant, Sam [Altman] is a constant, and I think that we are stronger because of that resilience and diversity." title: Bending Spoons skyrockets 41% as Berkshire Hathaway makes $330 million investment
content: Shares of Bending Spoons skyrocketed 41% after a new securities filing revealed that Berkshire Hathaway made a fresh $330 million investment into the company. The latest infusion follows the conglomerate's $600 million investment from July, when the Italy-based serial acquirer went public on the Nasdaq. Under the deal, Bending Spoons will issue 10 million ordinary shares to Berkshire at $33 a share. "Bending Spoons continuously evaluates M&A opportunities, and our pipeline remains strong," said Francesco Patarnello, Bending Spoons' co-founder and head of business acquisitions, in a statement. "We believe Berkshire Hathaway's investment reflects confidence in our team and Platform and will further enhance our financial flexibility and ability to pursue attractive acquisitions as part of our broader financing strategy." The investment now brings Berkshire's stake in the company to 4%, according to the filing, and is the conglomerate's latest investment decision as CEO Greg Abel took the helm from founder and legendary investor Warren Buffett at the start of the year.

title: 5 Things to Know
content: This is CNBC's Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox. Happy Wednesday. There's a strategy war brewing to win Gen Z's attention — and it involves everything from neon signs to dead mascots . Stock futures are lower this morning. The S&P 500 ended yesterday's session little changed . Here are five key things investors need to know to start the trading day: September's consumer price index — the closely followed basket of goods and services tracked by the Bureau of Labor Statistics — comes out this morning. It's the last CPI print before the midterm election, and economists are expecting it to show that price growth is reaccelerating. Here's what to know: Shares of Bank of America are more than 4% lower in premarket trading after the bank reported a steep drop in profit in the third quarter thanks to a $1.2 billion penalty from the U.S. Treasury Department. The company's revenue for the period also disappointed, coming in below Wall Street's estimates. The Treasury Department announced the ten-figure fine yesterday, saying the bank allegedly violated anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. The penalty weighed heavily on Bank of America's earnings, cutting income by 17 cents a share. As CNBC's Hugh Son writes, the fine could lead to questions about CEO Brian Moynihan's handle on the bank. Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley beat top- and bottom-line estimates this morning, posting equities trading revenue numbers that topped analysts' expectations by more than $900 million. Bank of America's Moynihan and Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick will both join CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" today. Watch live on CNBC or CNBC+. Anthropic is expected to disclose its third-quarter financials to a group of institutional investors today, two people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The meeting, set to be held at its San Francisco headquarters, comes as the Claude maker gears up for what could be a record-setting initial public offering. Revenue numbers from private AI giants have also become increasingly important for tech investors. Just last week, updated revenue figures from OpenAI sent stocks across the sector lower and raised questions about how Anthropic will account for sales and partner revenue. Speaking of OpenAI: The company and Department of Justice said yesterday that one of its employees was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was discovered in its executive conference room. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested in connection to the case last week, the DOJ said. Latino voters in South Texas surprised election watchers in 2024, when the historically Democratic-leaning group flipped for President Donald Trump. In next month's midterm election, they could be up for grabs. After their sweep in 2024, Republicans grew optimistic that they could continue to build on their momentum with Hispanic voters. But enthusiasm for the GOP appears to be waning amid concerns over inflation and immigration policy. CNBC's Justin Papp went to the Lone Star State to speak to these voters in South Texas, where three House races in majority-Hispanic border districts could decide which party controls Congress next year. Apple on Tuesday debuted its new home hub called HomeView . Priced at $299, the device has a seven-inch screen and is designed to sit a table or mount to a wall. It also can act as a smart hub for Apple devices across members of a household. As CNBC's Kif Lewsing writes, Apple appeared to use HomeView — as well as new Apple TV and HomePod hardware announced yesterday — as a showcase for its new Siri capabilities. The new products also mark Apple's first non-iPhone launch under new CEO John Ternus. title: Tech giants race to get AI gadgets on shelves for holiday rush
content: With the holidays just months away, tech companies are betting this is finally the year that AI starts showing up under the Christmas tree. Apple , Amazon and Microsoft have all announced new devices in the past week with the aim of bringing generative artificial intelligence firmly into the home. Nearly four years after the launch of ChatGPT, the leading consumer tech companies are touting improved personal assistants and speedier on-device chips with AI capabilities as they try to sell new laptops, tablets, phones and smart home computers. Success is far from guaranteed. In addition to the weakest consumer sentiment data in 12 years due largely to stubborn inflation, and growing fears about the potential safety risks of AI, there's a learning curve that comes with the new technology. Jitesh Ubrani, an analyst at IDC, said tech companies want to introduce AI to consumers to lay the groundwork for more aggressive device launches in the coming years. "This is really about getting devices into consumers' hands, into consumers' homes, slowly teaching them how to use it, and getting feedback from them," Ubrani said, adding that new gadgets from Apple, Amazon and Microsoft aren't expected to sell in large volumes, at least not yet. Getting affluent early adopters on board now could be considered a win given the macro headwinds. Hardware prices across the board have risen, driven by soaring costs for components, especially memory and storage, as power-hungry AI servers suck up most of the capacity. Those price hikes have led to plunging shipments this year of new smartphones and laptops. Microsoft kicked off the launches last week by showing off an Nvidia -powered Windows laptop starting at $2,599, based around an AI chip called RTX Spark that can run powerful AI without relying on the cloud. Amazon followed by releasing Alexa tablets , the company's first pieces of hardware named after its smart assistant. The largest Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs $550, compared to $155 for its predecessor, the Fire HD10. And on Tuesday of this week, Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub, powered by Siri AI. The $299 devices include a 7-inch screen that can be mounted, along with facial recognition software so it can be personalized for multiple family members. Analysts applauded Apple for introducing HomeView at a reasonable price given all the component shortages. "Apple has prioritized ecosystem adoption over immediate high hardware margins, delivering a local-AI hub at a price point that undercuts what a spec-heavy machine should logically cost," said Mohit Agrawal, who specializes in AI at CounterPoint Research, in an email. Dipanjan Chatterjee, an analyst at Forrester, said the shopping season will mark an early test of consumer demand for a new class of gadgets. "I think consumers are interested in what AI can do," said Chatterjee. "What's less clear is whether they are interested in buying hardware specifically because it is an AI device." Despite the many economic headwinds, the spending outlook heading into the holidays remains robust. Nearly half of U.S. consumers expect to spend the same or more this year compared to last year's holiday season, according to a McKinsey survey published in August. And Bain published a report last month, predicting that U.S. retail sales over the holidays will set new records and top $1 trillion for the first time. However, analysts cautioned "more than half of the nominal sales growth will come from higher inflation" pushing up prices. The firm predicted that sales in some electronics and appliances will remain flat. "In a time when folks are being a little money conscious, you say, 'Do I really need the next one of those, or could I drag out the replacement cycle on whatever it is?'" said Aaron Cheris, head of Bain's global retail practice, in an interview. "We've seen things that are discretionary purchases drag out longer." All three producers of the new AI gadgets emphasized their increasingly intelligent assistants, as well as more powerful chips to run them. Amazon said it's ditching the budget-friendly Fire family of devices in favor of three new Alexa Tablets that feature a more premium design with its souped-up AI assistant front and center. Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to summon the assistant and ask questions, get personalized recommendations or control their smart home. Amazon also introduced a hands-free mode, called "On-Screen Intelligence," that enables Alexa to read content on the tablet's display and take action, like preparing a shopping list based on a cooking video. Microsoft's new laptops with Nvidia chips can run AI coding models. Apple's HomeView uses Apple Intelligence to proactively show users their text messages, calendar appointments and photos. Apple expects users to talk to the device, and highlights Siri's ability to answer a broad range of questions, similar to the experience they have with modern chatbots. Apple also noted that HomeView uses the A18 chip, which was the fastest smartphone chip in the world when it was first introduced in September 2024. Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at researcher Creative Strategies, said companies will have to see if users are lured by the prospect of paying more for enhanced processing power. "Consumers out there are, I think, yet to be convinced that on-device matters as much, especially when you ask them to spend more for a device," Milanesi said. Ollama CEO Jeff Morgan said there's an audience for computers that give users control. His startup's open-source software allows people to install and use models on a variety of computers. "I think there's something about owning your AI versus renting it," he said. Then there's the longer-term opportunity that companies are pursuing, which involves getting consumers to buy subscriptions so they can lock in recurring revenue. Amazon's new Alexa requires a $19.99 monthly subscription, or Prime membership. Apple users have to buy an upgraded iCloud subscription to record secure video. Apple's biggest AI launch may come next week, when the company's new $1,999 iPhone Duo hits stores. The folding iPhone can display two apps side by side, including chats with Siri, offering a desktop-like interface for AI agents. WATCH: Amazon's Alexa tablets

title: ASML says it's getting order interest through 2030 as profit smashes expectations
content: ASML said Wednesday that some of its customers are expressing interest in placing orders for its critical semiconductor tools for 2029 and 2030 as the company reported third-quarter profit that beat expectations. The comments will likely comfort investors who have been looking to assess the longer-term demand outlook for ASML's lithography machines. "Our customers continue to increase their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts with us, driven primarily by their views on the size and duration of AI-related investments," CEO Christophe Fouquet said in a press release. "In light of their demand visibility, some customers are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030." ASML is the only company in the world that produces extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, a key tool used by the likes of TSMC to make the world's most advanced semiconductors. Investors closely watch the Dutch company's earnings for signs of AI-related chip demand. Fouquet said current supply planned for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of its customers. The company is "investigating ways" to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase it had previously forecast. ASML has now updated its guidance three times this year, upping its full-year forecast for the second time in July, and on Wednesday it raised the lower end of its sales forecast for 2026. The company now expects net sales of between 44 billion euros and 45 billion euros ($49.3 billion to $50.4 billion). The previous lower end of the forecast was for 43 billion euros. ASML also said it expects fourth-quarter net sales of between 14.2 billion euros and 15.2 billion euros. The upper end of the range is ahead of LSEG consensus estimates of 14.2 billion euros. ASML's stock was around 2% higher in early trade in Europe. Shares of the company have rallied 56% this year. During the quarter, Samsung and TSMC, the world's two biggest chipmakers, committed to using ASML's High NA extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. High NA EUV is ASML's next-generation tool, which analysts see as key to the Dutch firm's future growth. For the third quarter, here's how ASML did versus LSEG consensus estimates: The semiconductor equipment maker said it expects China sales to account for 20% of its total business, sticking to a prior forecast. While ASML holds an effective monopoly on EUV machines, a July report from The Information suggested an unnamed Chinese company had begun manufacturing an immersion deep ultraviolet lithography (DUV) machine, citing people familiar with the matter. ASML dominates the manufacturing of DUV machines, which are less advanced than EUV. China has been ramping up its domestic semiconductor supply chain, with some investors concerned it could challenge the European and U.S. dominance. However, analysts raised questions about China's ability to ramp up its own DUV technology. ASML meanwhile has faced challenges in China over the last few years. The company is restricted from selling EUV and some DUV tools to China.

title: Crypto bosses, CEOs and F1: Singapore's business events boom gathers pace
content: Billionaires, global CEOs and crypto executives descended on Singapore last week as a growing number of high-profile conferences coincided with the country's Formula 1 Grand Prix. More than 40 business events were held around this year's Grand Prix period, up from over 25 in 2025 and over 30 in 2024, according to the Singapore Tourism Board. The events included the Milken Institute Asia Summit, TOKEN2049, the Forbes Global CEO Conference, Solana Summit APAC and the Global-Asia Family Office Summit. Formula 1 has generated more than 2.2 billion Singapore dollars ($1.72 billion) in incremental tourism receipts between its debut in 2008 and 2024, according to Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry , which equates to an average of S$150 million each. The race itself costs approximately S$140 million a year to organize, METI said, though noted it isn't directly comparable with the revenue generated. Singapore GP said the 2026 race drew 301,294 spectators, the second-highest attendance in the event's history. Business events themselves are becoming a larger source of tourism revenue. Receipts from meetings, incentives, conventions and exhibitions (MICE) rose 35% to S$2.3 billion in 2025, outpacing the 10% growth in Singapore's overall tourism receipts to a record S$32.8 billion, data from STB showed. Singapore's Tourism Board noted that MICE visitors typically spend significantly more than leisure travelers. Organizers are increasingly capitalizing on the excitement surrounding Formula 1 to extend delegates' stays, according to Poh Chi Chuan, executive director of exhibitions and conferences at STB. "This creates a natural gravitational pull, when the city is buzzing and the right target audience is already flying in, savvy planners build on that momentum," Poh said. At TOKEN2049, one of the world's major cryptocurrency conferences, overseas attendees accounted for 85.6% of participants this year, up from 82.7% in 2025, according to figures provided by the event organizer. The figures classify overseas attendees as those who are not Singaporean nationals. Chinese attendees accounted for 11.8% of participants, nearly double the 6% share recorded last year, overtaking Americans as the largest group. The influx of business travelers also coincided with strong demand at Singapore's luxury hotels. Marina Bay Sands said its hotel, the iconic three-towered building often featured in photos of the Singapore skyline, operated at near-full occupancy during the Formula 1 period. The integrated resort also hosted TOKEN2049 at its Expo & Convention Centre, underscoring how major business conferences and sporting events are increasingly overlapping. For the hotel industry overall, the clustering of MICE events and Formula 1 helped propel rates to record levels last year. In October 2025, average room rates rose 19.5% from a year earlier to S$384.15, according to hospitality data provider CoStar . On the opening day of that race weekend, hotel occupancy reached 95.9% and the average room rate jumped to S$757.62.

A giant elephant’s tooth has preserved clues to the watery world that sustained early humans nearly 700,000 years ago. Researchers studying elephant remains from Gesher Benot Ya’aqov (GBY-NBA) in northern Israel have reconstructed a Pleistocene environment rich in water, vegetation, and wildlife. Published in Quaternary Science Reviews , the study reveals the landscape shared by enormous mammals and some of the region’s earliest human toolmakers. Led by Hannah Farrell (a PhD candidate at Haifa University), the research examined molar and tusk fragments excavated by Prof. Gonen Sharon of Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and his colleagues. The site, Gesher Benot Ya’aqov (Daughters of Jacob Bridge), sits in the Jordan Rift Valley, south of today’s Hula Valley. The fossils belonged to Palaeoloxodon antiquus , the straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Pleistocene. Nearby basalt handaxes and cleavers place early humans in the same setting. These tools belong to the Acheulian tradition, among the earliest and most geographically widespread stone tool technologies in human history. The tooth offered more than a way to identify the animal. Its structure, microscopic wear, and chemical composition provided different lines of evidence about its life and surroundings. The team combined CT scanning, 3D reconstruction, microscopic wear analysis, isotope geochemistry, and pollen studies to piece together the broader ecosystem. The results point to an enduring landscape of woodlands, grasslands, marshes, rivers, and shallow-water habitats. Carbon isotope values suggest that the elephant lived where water remained consistently available. Pollen recovered from sediments added detail to that picture, revealing reeds, sedges, willows, tamarisks, and aquatic plants. Together, the findings suggest that the Hula Valley region was a stable ecological refuge within the Levantine Corridor, the land bridge connecting Africa and Eurasia. Reliable water and biological resources likely made this landscape a valuable stopping point or habitat for wildlife and human groups moving through the region. According to Sharon, “understanding how humans and animals responded to environmental change hundreds of thousands of years ago helps us better understand the forces that shaped our species.” “The availability of water, vegetation, and animal resources shaped where humans and wildlife could survive,” Sharon says. “The wetlands, rivers, and woodlands of the Hula Valley helped sustain life along one of the world’s earliest migration corridors, offering a rare opportunity to understand the ecological conditions that supported both animals and human populations nearly 700,000 years ago.” Reference: “Elephant dental remains from the Acheulian site at North Bridge Acheulian–Gesher Benot Ya’aqov: hominin behavior and environmental implications” by Hannah Farrell, Gonen Sharon, Minji Jin, Dafna Langgut, Cheryl A. Makarewicz and Nimrod Marom, 14 September 2026, Quaternary Science Reviews . DOI: 10.1016/j.quascirev.2026.110277 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .

Once pushed to the brink, giant tortoises on a Seychelles atoll now outnumber the country’s people, with a new survey estimating nearly 183,000 animals. Aldabra Atoll, home to the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population, supports an estimated 180,000 animals, according to research led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter. The highest estimate yet for the Aldabra giant tortoise ( Aldabrachelys gigantea ) reflects both a remarkable conservation recovery and a better way of counting animals that are difficult to see. Published in Ecology and Evolution , the study analyzed monitoring records collected by SIF staff from 2018 through 2022. It delivers the first rigorous estimate covering the atoll and replaces the widely quoted figure of about 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s. The team’s best estimate was almost 183,000 adult and subadult tortoises, more than the entire human population of the Seychelles. Their numbers appeared relatively stable during the study period. That abundance would have been difficult to imagine in the 19th century, when heavy exploitation reduced Aldabra’s tortoises to fewer than 1,000. Their recovery has been supported by decades of protection, including the atoll’s designation as a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Today, Aldabra and the Galapagos are the two remaining strongholds of native wild giant tortoises, with far fewer animals in the Galapagos. The new findings strengthen Aldabra’s reputation as one of the Indian Ocean’s outstanding conservation successes. “The monitoring data in this study were collected by SIF staff living and working on the atoll, year after year. More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra,” said Dr. Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF. The larger total comes with an important qualification: it does not mean the population has nearly doubled since 1999. A tortoise can be present without being visible, and earlier surveys did not adequately account for animals concealed in scrub or shade. Those estimates probably missed a substantial number. To address that problem, the researchers used Bayesian hierarchical distance sampling. This statistical method accounts for animals that observers failed to detect and for differences in visibility across habitats. It produces an estimate of the population, rather than simply a tally of sightings. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring program is one of the longest-running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said study co-author Dr. Nancy Bunbury. “By modeling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.” The animals were most concentrated in Aldabra’s grasslands, known as “tortoise turf.” The next highest densities occurred on open exposed surfaces and in open mixed scrub. Dense scrub, mangroves, and Pemphis vegetation made tortoises harder to detect. Correcting for those differences helps researchers distinguish places with fewer animals from places where animals are simply harder to spot. Together, the findings describe a population that has recovered dramatically from historical exploitation and now appears healthy and stable. They also establish a more dependable starting point for measuring future changes, something direct comparisons with older estimates cannot provide. Despite their recovery, Aldabra’s tortoises face growing environmental pressures. Droughts are projected to become longer and more frequent, reducing food and shade, while rising seas threaten the atoll’s low-lying habitats. Feral goats, which devastated Aldabra’s vegetation, were eradicated in 2012. But feral cats and black rats remain and prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The researchers say planned efforts to eliminate these mammals could allow more young tortoises to survive, support further population growth, and help the species withstand climate pressures. “These results are great news for the tortoises and a testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr. Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter in Cornwall who helped develop the statistical framework used to analyze the monitoring data. “But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline, not an endpoint. Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought, and invasive species.” Reference: “Inferring the Abundance of an Island Megaherbivore From Semi-Structured Distance Sampling” by Lara B. Hillyard, Nancy Bunbury, Christopher N. Kaiser-Bunbury, Dave Hodgson, Luke A’Bear, Cheryl L. Sanchez, Christopher W. Jones, April Burt, Frauke Fleischer-Dogley and Dave W. Hudson, 4 September 2026, Ecology and Evolution . DOI: 10.1002/ece3.74282 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .

One of the world’s rarest rhinos faces a devastating problem: finding another of its kind before it is too late. Small, hairy, and cheekily charismatic. Those words sprung to mind when I first met a Sumatran rhinoceros ( Dicerorhinus sumatrensis ) after traversing the maze of wooden slatted paths at the conservation center in the dense, humid forests of Malaysian Borneo. It was 1998, and I was an eager student volunteer at the center. At that time, 300 Sumatran rhinos were thought to exist globally. I saw this female rhino as a symbol of conservation hope. But today, according to the International Rhino Foundation’s 2026 State of the Rhino report, less than 50 Sumatran rhinos remain. All are found in Indonesia. The Javan rhino ( Rhinoceros sondaicus ) is just as rare. While these figures rely on estimates, the trajectory is alarming. So what is driving this decline? And how can we protect the few Sumatran and Javan rhinos that are left? In modern culture, rhinos represent strength , power, and security. We use them as sports mascots and feature them in everything from car logos to safety equipment brands. Their ubiquity in popular culture may lead us to underestimate the urgency of their plight. Species used as marketing emblems are often considered more common than they truly are. There are five surviving species of rhinos. I have had the privilege of getting to know all but one while working as a wildlife veterinarian in zoos, sanctuaries, and the wild. Africa is home to white and black rhinos, whose populations have fluctuated greatly throughout history. The water-loving greater one-horned rhino lives in India and Nepal and has seen a steady recovery from near extinction in the early 1900s. These three species can be found in zoos and tend to get the most public attention. Compared to their African and Indian relatives, Sumatran and Javan rhinos typically fly under the radar. However, their critically endangered status signals these animals are in urgent need of assistance. According to the latest State of the Rhino report, the future of the elusive Javan rhino and the small, hairy Sumatran rhino is now especially precarious. Distribution is a major reason why. There are roughly 50 surviving Javan rhinos. All live in a single protected area, Ujung Kulon National Park, on the island of Java. Due to nearby converging tectonic plates, it is vulnerable to earthquakes and tsunamis . One natural disaster could well exterminate the Javan rhino population. In contrast, the several dozen remaining Sumatran rhinos are scattered into many subpopulations, across two islands. This means the chance of a wild individual rhino encountering another of their kind is remote or even impossible. With no prospect of finding a compatible mate, isolated survivors are destined to be the end of their genetic line . To protect this fragmented population, the International Rhino Foundation established the Sumatran Rhino Sanctuary in 1996. It is located in Way Kambas National Park on the island of Sumatra. The sanctuary is currently home to ten intensively managed , semi-captive Sumatran rhinos. The resident animals live in large, natural rainforest habitats. They are provided with nutrition, security, and regular veterinary care. Increasing rhino numbers through natural or assisted breeding requires patience. Females give birth to a single calf after about 16 months of pregnancy. It may be several years before they have another. Infertility is a recognized problem in some rhinos . The sanctuary has had some hard-won successes. Five Sumatran rhino calves were born there between 2012 and 2023, in part due to close reproductive management and monitoring . Excitingly, authorities have just announced two new pregnancies. Camera-trap footage has also confirmed the births of up to five Javan rhino calves in Ujung Kulon in recent years. These precious births go some way towards recovery of these two species. Poaching is a persistent threat to all rhino species. Worryingly, global demand for rhino horn is increasing, especially in China and Vietnam. Besides its long-standing use in traditional medicine, rhino horn now plays a role in demonstrating wealth and status, particularly in business circles. Poachers killed as many as 26 Javan rhinos between 2019 and 2023 alone. Anti-poaching strategies include behavior change campaigns , which focus on promoting social and cultural unacceptability of horn use and purchase. Governments may also rely on intelligence-led law enforcement and disruption to large crime syndicates to stop poachers. While poaching convictions and court sentences are increasing, including in Indonesia , this is not enough to keep the world’s rhinos safe. Proactive measures, such as protecting and restoring habitat suitable for each species, are vital to the recovery of rhino populations. This is particularly true as humans increasingly encroach on wild places. Translocation —capturing and then releasing animals in a new place—is one possible way of protecting the world’s rhinos. Recent research examined whether this strategy could be used to re-establish populations of Sumatran and Javan rhinos across their former range throughout Southeast Asia. Conservation authorities can learn from past translocations of African rhinos, which show finding suitable habitat , anti-poaching protection, and careful planning are crucial to the success of these efforts. More broadly, effective rhino conservation relies on having an army of supporters. Local communities should tangibly benefit from living alongside rhinos, for example through job creation and by sharing in the proceeds of ecotourism. Even from afar, people can help by supporting conservation organizations and avoiding the purchase of products that contribute to tropical deforestation. Sustainable funding and political commitment are crucial to protecting the few Indonesian rhinos that remain. It’s my wish that younger generations, including my future students, have the privilege of meeting a small, hairy rhinoceros for themselves. Adapted from an article originally published in The Conversation . Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .

title: World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
content: Archaeologists working off the coast of Turkey have found a shipwreck dating back around 4,700 years, making it the oldest in the world. A number of ancient storage vessels known as amphorae were recovered during excavations at the wreck, which was found at a depth of around 100 feet near Kekova Island off the coast of southern Turkey, according to a statement from the country’s culture ministry, published Wednesday. The amphorae date from 4,400-4,700 years ago and provide new information on maritime history, the daily lives of mariners and trade connections at the time. The vessels are thought to mainly have been used for transporting olive oil or wine. However, one amphora features a distinctive set of marks and two holes in its body, which suggest it could have been used to make cheese or butter. Researchers said the presence of this amphora may mean that sailors took goats with them on their voyages, using their milk to make dairy products. The excavations were led by Hakan Öniz, a professor at Akdeniz University, Antalya, who told CNN that the shipwreck was first discovered four years ago. The amphorae were initially thought to be much more recent, but then Öniz read a publication on amphorae that had been found near the Giza pyramids in Egypt — the oldest of which was believed to have been under construction at the same time as the ship sank. “These resembled the amphorae in our shipwreck,” Öniz told CNN on Wednesday, adding that a team of researchers made a follow-up dive at the site. They then invited a leading expert on amphorae, Australian archaeologist Karin Sowada, to visit the shipwreck and examine the evidence. “We reached a consensus and proceeded with further analysis,” said Öniz, who added the team are “generally confident” that this is the oldest shipwreck in the world. “It is not just the amphorae; the anchors and other artifacts found at the shipwreck site also point to the same centuries,” he said. Turkey’s culture and tourism minister, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, said the amphorae appear to have moved around the Eastern Mediterranean. “Clay analyses indicate that the amphorae were likely produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley,” Ersoy said in the statement. “The fact that similar examples have been found in Egypt, Troy, and Crete is of great importance for understanding the trade networks that connected different geographies via sea routes,” he said. Researchers believe the ship may have been traveling from the Levantine coast, which runs from Turkey in the north to Egypt in the south, to Troy or Crete when it was wrecked.

title: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections
content:
A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​
Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country.
"This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast", the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.
The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.
Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it.
"I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC.
A new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators.
Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.
There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by Pew Research Center.
Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.
Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand.
"This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."
Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US Senator working on data centre legislation.
"There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."
That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.
Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".
His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.
The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.
During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.
Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the push back against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago.

title: Palantir drops City Hall legal fight over Met deal
content:
Palantir has dropped its High Court challenge against the mayor of London's policing office over a blocked £50m deal with the Metropolitan Police.
However, the Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC) has not reversed its decision to stop the Met agreeing a two-year software contract with the US technology firm.
Instead, in a joint statement on Wednesday, it said the decision was "not based on Palantir's values or ethics" and that the company was "free and welcomed" to bid when the contract is re-run.
The mayor's office said neither side had made any payment to the other and both would pay their own legal costs.
London mayor Lord Sadiq Khan said: "Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organisations across the UK and beyond."
In Wednesday's joint statement, MOPAC acknowledged that a statement from the mayor's spokesman provided to the media "could have incorrectly created the impression" that the firm's values had been a factor.
"MOPAC is happy to correct any contrary impression," it said, adding that it "does not have, and has never had, any policy of not contracting with Palantir".
It said its decision had been based on its legal duty to examine spending proposals and ensure value for money, and that it was working with the Met to re-run the contract "with all due expediency".
The case had been due to go to trial in January, and Lord Khan had agreed to have his text messages and emails searched as part of it.
MOPAC blocked the deal for AI tools to automate intelligence analysis in criminal investigations in May.
In a letter to the commissioner, deputy mayor for policing and crime Kaya Comer-Schwartz said the Met had only seriously considered one supplier, and that its failure to seek MOPAC's approval for its procurement strategy was a "clear and serious breach" of the rules.
Palantir filed a lawsuit in June, arguing that MOPAC had imposed an "unlawful veto" by wrongly taking its "values and ethics" into account, which MOPAC denied.
Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said in June that the force's process had been "legally and commercially compliant" and warned that services and staff might have to be cut.
He told the London Policing Board the Palantir system would have allowed the Met to cut 500 jobs in response to a budget shortfall of £100m this year and £125m next year.
The force's 2026-27 budget included plans to cut 1,150 jobs, with the work of 500 of those to be done by AI tools to speed up intelligence reports and the analysis of mobile phones.
Sir Mark also said that in March 2026 the Met had fewer officers per 100,000 people than at any point since 1981.

title: Patients' frustration at GP surgery's AI receptionist
content:
Patients have described their "frustration" in dealing with a new AI receptionist tool at their GP surgery, which some said was a "wall" to receiving care.
Newbury Street Practice, in Wantage, Oxfordshire, began using the AI Andi triage system in July, with all calls made to the surgery passing through the bot.
A spokesperson for the surgery said majority of feedback regarding the new system had been positive, and that it would "improve access" and "increase capacity".
But patient Jo Rogers is one of those who have criticised the system and said the AI bot "puts you off ever bothering" contacting the practice.
"I had to get through AI Andy's 'wall' recently," Rogers said.
She said she had been waiting in a phone queue for 20 minutes, after which "he decided he couldn't help me".
All calls to the surgery go through the AI system, which can then pass them onto a human receptionist, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
In an introduction post about the system, the practice website said Andi "listens carefully, understands how you're feeling, and helps you get what you need quickly".
But some patients have raised their concerns. Among them is 65-year-old Tricia Lockhart, who said she was left "frustrated" after the AI system thought she was "calling about pregnancy".
"Quite an achievement for a 65-year-old," she said.
A spokesperson for the surgery said the purpose of introducing the technology was "to improve access, increase capacity and allow staff to spend more time supporting patients who are unable or choose not to use our digital options".
But user John Allinson disagreed, saying: "AI is all about cutting costs and saving money." The GP practice disputes this claim.
Local MP Olly Glover recently contributed to the debate, after being contacted by residents in his Didcot and Wantage constituency.
He said he had been in touch with the GP surgery who "like many other surgeries, are trying to streamline their administrative processes".
"There is clearly pressure on primary care services across our constituency, where we have seen high levels of housing growth," he said.
"Successive governments have not taken the need to provide health and other infrastructure ahead of new homes seriously enough."
In the first month of its installation, a spokesperson for Newbury Street Surgery said feedback on the AI tool had been "79% positive".
"We know some patients, particularly those less confident with technology, have found the change harder, and as with any new system it takes time to settle," they said.
"We continue to review our processes, systems and feedback regularly post implementation to shape next steps including any future support our patients may require. "

title: Vehicle thefts rise to highest level in a decade
content:
Vehicle thefts in Devon and Cornwall have risen to their highest level in at least a decade, with police linking the increase to organised criminal gangs and increasingly sophisticated theft techniques.
Devon and Cornwall Police recorded 1,550 vehicle theft offences in 2025-26, up 60.8% from 964 in 2015-16 and up 11.4% from 1,392 in 2024-25, Home Office data shows.
Police said organised crime groups were responsible for a significant proportion of vehicle thefts, with offenders increasingly using technology such as electronic key cloning to steal vehicles.
Despite a recent drop, vehicle thefts are up almost 50% in England and Wales compared with a decade ago, according to the figures.
Vehicle thefts in Devon and Cornwall remained relatively stable between 2015-16 and 2020-21, when there were 964 and 955 offences respectively, before climbing sharply to 1,491 offences in 2022-23. Although offences fell slightly to 1,392 in 2024-25, they rose again to 1,550 in 2025-26.
Det Ch Supt Ben Deer from the force, said: "The increase in vehicle theft offences is being driven by a range of factors, many of which are being seen across the UK."
Organised crime groups are thought to be responsible for a significant proportion of thefts, targeting vehicles for resale, dismantling them for parts or moving them through wider criminal networks.
Theft methods have also become increasingly sophisticated, with offenders using technology such as electronic key cloning and signal amplification to "bypass modern vehicle security systems", Deer said.
Vehicles could often be stolen quickly while leaving few forensic opportunities for investigators.
"The rising value of used vehicles and vehicle parts has also made this type of offending more profitable," he said.
He also said vehicle theft investigations had become more complex because offenders often operated across force boundaries.
"Devon and Cornwall Police remains committed to pursuing all available lines of inquiry and bringing offenders to justice wherever the evidence supports it," he said.
Devon and Cornwall Police has its own advice on how to deter vehicle thieves.
Sgt Owen Messenger, from the force's road casualty reduction team, said vehicle owners can take simple steps to make themselves less of a target.
He said one of the easiest ways to protect keyless vehicles was to keep keys in a Faraday pouch or box, which blocks the electronic signal that thieves can use to gain access to a car.
He also suggested keeping keys away from front doors, where criminals may be able to amplify the signal from outside a property.
He also recommended aftermarket immobilisers and alarm systems to make a vehicle as difficult and time-consuming to steal as possible.
"Essentially you're trying to make it more and more difficult for the thief to take your car," he said.
"The longer it takes them to do it, the less likely they are to try and do it, because there's more chance of them getting caught."
Messenger said he personally fitted aftermarket security systems to cars he believed were at greater risk of theft because he considered the extra expense worthwhile to protect his investment.

title: The genetic technique that finds (almost) every infection
content:
It identified Covid-19. Now this genetic technique is helping doctors to make life-or-death decisions.
In late December 2019, a team of virologists from three major Chinese cities began analysing swabs taken from patients hospitalised with mysterious cases of severe pneumonia.
All had been present at the Huanan Seafood Market, Wuhan, before rapidly falling unwell. But when the virologists ran the samples, they drew a blank: the genetic material did not match any previously discovered pathogen.
The doctors turned to a new screening method known as metagenomic testing. Instead of checking for known microbes, the test could reveal all the microorganisms present in the samples – previously identified or not.
It enabled them to see that the pathogen in the patients' samples bore a close resemblance to the coronavirus family, a group that included viruses which had previously caused outbreaks of severe pneumonia in humans, such as Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (Mers). The scientists had just discovered Covid-19.
"It was a gamechanger compared with previous pandemics," says Niranjan Nagarajan, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore. Knowing what the pathogen was made it possible to rapidly develop Covid diagnostics to try to curb the spread, and kickstarted the frantic search for treatments and vaccines around the globe .
This remains the best-known use of metagenomics to date. But the test is now increasingly being used in hospitals. And from quickly diagnosing sepsis to identifying the causes of unexplained ailments, it's already saving lives.
Whenever a patient arrives in a neurological ward displaying signs of confusion and drowsiness, and complaining of fever, headache and weakness, doctors are acutely aware that it could be a life-or-death emergency.
How metagenomic testing works
Metagenomics, the study of all the DNA and RNA found in a particular environment, is seen as an increasingly important clinical approach . Metagenomic testing involves extracting genetic material from a sample, then using advanced sequencing methods to identify the genetic codes of everything that's there. These results can be analysed by computers with reference to large databases, allowing doctors to pinpoint the exact organisms present, such as bacteria or viruses.
This constellation of symptoms can indicate meningitis or encephalitis – deadly conditions affecting the brain and spinal cord. Yet doctors often face a critical dilemma. The most suitable treatment would depend on whether the patient's condition was due to a virus or bacteria, or an overreaction from the brain's immune system. With limited tests and time, however, doctors are often forced to hedge their bets.
"You need to make a decision immediately," says Charles Chiu, a professor and infectious diseases expert at the University of California San Francisco Department of Medicine in the US, who has been carrying out new studies into the use of metagenomic tests. "Currently, with patients who are critically ill, doctors treat them for infection and for autoimmune disease."
In some ways, this is contradictory, because it involves suppressing the patient's immune system even though they might have an infection. "But there's often no other choice," says Chiu.
Metagenomics is now helping to inform these decisions. Chiu and his colleagues have developed a pioneering metagenomics test for identifying pathogens within cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid that bathes the brain and spinal cord. The test has already flagged cases where, unbeknownst to doctors, a pathogen was driving a patient's symptoms.
For example, Chiu encountered a patient who had been diagnosed with meningitis and liver failure, and was scheduled to receive a liver transplant. But the metagenomics test on her spinal fluid revealed that she was actually infected with the hepatitis E virus. While hepatitis E is a known and treatable cause of liver disease, it is not commonly tested for in high-income countries such as the US.
"We gave her an antiviral medication, she got better, and we spared her from undergoing the transplant," says Chiu.
Until recently, the use of metagenomics has been limited by the length of time required for the analysis. Separating human and microbial DNA, and identifying the signs of a potentially worrisome pathogen, requires highly specialist skills. "Doing the sequencing and the analysis can take several days to a week," says Nagarajan. "The patient might die before you're able to get a result."
Now, though, machines can sequence DNA within as little as one to two hours, and AI tools can ingest vast datasets to decipher patterns within them. And it's finally making metagenomics more widely accessible.
For people with poorly functioning immune systems, any infection can swiftly turn into a potentially deadly threat. Transplant recipients, cancer patients undergoing immune-suppressing treatment and those living with autoimmune diseases must be on constant high alert.
Studies have suggested that immunosuppressed patients who develop sepsis or blood poisoning due to an infection are at a 23% higher risk of dying in hospital. However, making a quick diagnosis in these cases is not always easy.

title: Broadband fears after fibre works stop in village
content:
Residents in a rural Kent village have raised concerns they could be left without broadband access after fibre installation works stopped.
Work began in August in Hunton to replace existing copper broadband infrastructure with fibre cables, but residents said it stopped after a few days.
Some residents said they had been told they might need to find another broadband provider, but they did not know what was happening.
Kings Hill-based firm Trooli said it had not been possible to extend its fibre network and affected customers had been contacted. Openreach said the old network would close on 31 January 2027 and customers would need to move to a digital phone service by then.
Resident Rodney Ballard told the Local Democracy Reporting Service that Trooli had given notice to some residents that their connections would be terminated, while Openreach had said copper connections would be withdrawn.
"There's no real plan being told to residents how this is going to happen," he said.
Hunton parish and Maidstone borough councillor Mike Summersgill said residents had welcomed the start of installation work but then "all of a sudden the road closure and barriers were taken away".
After work stopped, he said: "My worry is for the single, elderly constituents who rely purely on the landline to keep in touch with family or to be talked to by doctors."
Leah Istratescu, from Staplehurst, who works at Hunton and Linton Pre-School, said reliable broadband was essential for running the school and communicating with parents, adding: "It's really important that we keep them updated."
A Trooli spokesperson said the broadband service had been delivered using Openreach copper infrastructure that was being withdrawn.
The company said it had explored extending its fibre network, but said: "Unfortunately, there are few locations where, because of excessive costs, we have had to conclude this is simply not possible."
Trooli said it had contacted affected customers and advised them of other broadband options.
After some customers said they had been told the copper broadband switch-off would be on 23 October, an Openreach spokesperson said: "Openreach has no plans to switch off services supporting broadband or phone lines in the village this October."
They said: "Decisions about Trooli's services or its fibre rollout in Hunton are for the company and are separate from the closure of the analogue phone network.
"Anyone concerned about their service should speak to their communications provider - the company they pay their bill to - about the options available."
The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said rural communities should not be left behind in the rollout of faster broadband.
It said: "We are investing billions of pounds to bring internet upgrades to hard-to-reach homes and businesses that would otherwise miss out - including in Kent.
"Where commercial rollout plans change, the government will work with suppliers to explore alternative ways to connect affected communities."
